citation: README.md desiderata, agent states are the point and attention routing; docs/architecture.md, ownership of truth and one action path
why:
The view says what is on screen. The roster says what exists, which is the other half of the founding desideratum - and the more important half for attention, because a pane no window is showing is the one most likely to have finished without anybody noticing.

Two decisions live here and both are why it is in the core rather than the sidebar. What order a person reads the panes in, and what a pane is called when `w1:p2` tells them nothing. A shell that sorted and named for itself would be a second place those answers live, and the CLI and the agent-facing API would each grow a third.

The list is a tree - daemon, then tab, then pane - because a flat list of panes cannot say which of them sit side by side in one tab, and a window shows one tab per region, so the tab is the thing a person navigates between. The numbering runs across the whole window rather than restarting at each machine, so that the third caption down the sidebar, ⌘3, and two presses of next-tab all mean one tab.

The rendering below is one line per tab and one line per pane, in list order, so a case that gets the order wrong reads as obviously wrong rather than as a set that happens to differ.

cases.name: panes read in the order their tab lays them out
cases.why: The list runs down the side of a window whose panes run across it, and the eye moves between the two constantly. Sorting by id instead would be stable and would disagree with the screen for any tab somebody has rearranged, which is every tab after the first split.

cases.name: a tab whose tree has not arrived still lists its panes
cases.why: A tree is published on its own event and arrives after the panes do, so this is an ordinary moment on the way up rather than a fault. Hiding a pane until its arrangement is known would empty the list at exactly the moment a window is being opened onto running work.

cases.name: a tree that disagrees with its tab does not lose a pane from the list
cases.why: The view withholds a disagreeing tree rather than repairing it, because rendering one would tear down surfaces. A list has no surfaces to lose and the opposite failure: a pane missing from the roster is a pane nobody can be routed to. So the panes decide what exists and the tree only decides order, which is the same rule read the other way round.

cases.name: a pane is named by its directory and the harness in it
cases.why:
The two things that tell coding-agent panes apart when nobody has said otherwise. The id says nothing to anybody; the directory answers 'which project' and the harness answers 'which of these is running claude', which are the two questions a list like this gets asked.

This used to argue that a terminal title is whatever the program last felt like setting, and therefore worth nothing. That was wrong about coding agents, which set it to what they are working on, and it is now the second line of the row. It stays off the first line for the reason the old wording was reaching for: a title changes as work happens, and the line you learn a pane by should not.

panes: local/w1:p1 place=1 tab=w1:t1 label="muster · claude" hidden

cases.name: a pane running no agent is named by its directory alone
cases.why: Most panes in a window are a shell somebody left open. Appending an empty harness would leave a trailing separator on the majority of rows, and inventing one would claim a detection nobody made.

cases.name: a pane with no directory falls back to its id
cases.why: An id nobody can read beats a blank row nobody can point at. A daemon that reports no cwd - or reports the filesystem root, which names nothing - still holds a pane somebody may need to reach.

cases.name: a trailing slash is not a directory name
cases.why: A daemon is free to report either spelling of the same directory, and a row reading `""` for one and `src` for the other would be the same pane looking like two different bugs.

cases.name: a pane a region is showing says so
cases.why: The whole point of the list. A pane already on screen wants pointing at, and a pane nowhere on screen wants surfacing - two different things to do, and the row has to say which.

cases.name: daemons come in the order their regions sit in the window
cases.why: The list reads down the side in the order the panes read across it. Sorting by daemon id would be stable and arbitrary - it would put a devenv above a laptop for no reason a person looking at the window could see, and every glance would cost a translation.

cases.name: a daemon with no region on screen comes after the ones that have
cases.why: It still belongs on the list - its panes are exactly the ones nobody is looking at. Last rather than first, because the part of the list that maps onto the window should be the part that reads in the window's order.

cases.name: a daemon that has said nothing yet contributes no rows
cases.why: An attached daemon whose subscription has not bootstrapped holds no panes this process knows of, and inventing rows for it would show a session nobody has. It is an ordinary moment on the way up, not a failure, so it is silence rather than a placeholder.

cases.name: two daemons that hand out the same pane id are two rows
cases.why: Every daemon names its first pane `w1:p1`. A list keyed by pane alone would collapse a laptop's and a devenv's into one row, and clicking it would send somebody to the wrong machine - the failure attention routing can least afford.

cases.name: tabs are numbered across the window, not within each daemon
cases.why: The number is the place in the list a person is looking at, and that list spans machines - a window showing a laptop beside a devenv is the arrangement this project exists for. Restarting at each daemon would give two tabs the same number, so two captions would read alike and next_tab would walk an order the sidebar does not show. Panes are counted the same way and for the same reason; the difference is that theirs is what ⌘N names and this one only names the tab.

cases.name: a tab is on screen when a region shows it, whatever its panes are doing
cases.why: Two different questions, and a zoomed tab is where they come apart: the region is showing the tab, and the tree inside it renders one pane while the rest are not on screen. A tab marked hidden because its panes were would tell somebody to go somewhere they are already looking.

cases.name: a tab in a daemon holding several workspaces is named by the workspace
cases.why: herdr labels a workspace with its directory and labels a tab with its number inside that workspace, so `1` on its own tells two projects' first tabs apart not at all. The workspace is the useful half of a tab's name and goes in front of it - but only when there is more than one, because repeating one project's name down every row of the list says nothing and costs a word off every label.

cases.name: a tab nobody has named is called after its place in the window
cases.why:
herdr labels an unnamed tab with its position inside its workspace, so the second tab's label is literally `2`, and two daemons would each contribute a `1`. That is not a name, so it is dropped - and something has to take its place, because the caption is now the whole of the row. Muster writes `Tab <place>` from its own numbering, which counts across the window and so cannot collide.

This used to be empty, back when a number was drawn beside every caption. The numbers moved onto the pane rows, and an empty caption became a row with nothing on it at all - which is worse than a wrong one, because there is nothing to notice.

cases.name: stepping forward from the last tab of one daemon lands on the first of the next
cases.why: The order spans machines, so this is the step that says so. A walk that stopped at a daemon boundary would leave the other machine's tabs unreachable whenever no region was on it - which is exactly the case this exists for, since a window showing a laptop beside a devenv is the arrangement the project is built around.

cases.name: stepping forward off the end of the list comes back to the start
cases.why: Between them, next and previous have to reach every tab - that reachability is the whole reason these exist, since a pane in a tab no region shows can otherwise be reached only by mouse and the mouse's list can be put away. A step that silently did nothing at the end is indistinguishable from a dead key.

cases.name: stepping back off the start of the list comes round to the end
cases.why: The same guarantee read the other way. Wrapping in one direction and stopping in the other would make the pair asymmetric for no reason a person could predict.

cases.name: stepping from a tab that is not in the list goes to the end it came from
cases.why: An ordinary moment rather than a bug: nothing is focused yet, or the tab closed from another client while the keystroke was in flight. Refusing would leave a chord that does nothing and says nothing, so a step from nowhere enters the list at the end it was travelling from.

cases.name: stepping back from nowhere enters the list at its end
cases.why: The mirror of entering at the start. Whichever end a step from nowhere lands on, it has to be the one that direction came from, or the first press of a chord goes the opposite way to every press after it.

cases.name: a number names the pane at that place, counting from one
cases.why:
What ⌘3 means. Counting from one rather than zero because the sidebar counts that way and the keyboard has no zero next to the one - and the number a person reads off a row has to be the number that takes them there.

The count runs across daemons and across tabs alike, so the third numbered row is the third pane in the window rather than the third on some machine. Here that lands on a pane the second daemon holds, in a tab nothing is showing: focusing a pane surfaces the tab holding it, so the numbers reach every tab through the panes in it and no tab needs a chord of its own.

cases.name: a number past the last pane names nothing
cases.why: Doing nothing beats landing somewhere. Clamping to the last pane would make ⌘9 mean a different pane every time one opened or closed, which is a chord nobody can build a habit on - and the honest answer to 'go to the ninth pane' in a window of four is that there isn't one.

cases.name: an agent's own title is the second line of its row
cases.why:
The founding promise is that fifteen agents can be told apart at a glance, and fifteen rows reading `<directory> · claude` cannot do it: they say where a session lives, never what it is doing. A harness already publishes what it is doing as its terminal title, so nothing has to be invented - only carried and drawn.

In the core rather than in the sidebar because it is a decision, and the CLI and an agent asking what the window holds must get the same answer as the person reading it.

panes: local/w1:p1 place=1 tab=w1:t1 label="muster · claude" subtitle="first working build" hidden

cases.name: a pane with no harness gets no second line, whatever it calls itself
cases.why:
A shell sets a title too. oh-my-zsh's default is `<user>@<host>:<path>`, which is the row's own first line spelled longer, and most panes in a window are a shell somebody left open - so a rule of 'draw it when it exists' would double the height of the list to repeat it.

Requiring a detected harness is a fact the daemon reports, where suppressing shell titles by shape would be a guess about somebody's dotfiles. The cost is real and is accepted here rather than hidden: a pane running something that titles itself usefully, which herdr recognized no agent in, stays on one line.

cases.name: a title that only repeats the row is not drawn twice
cases.why:
Claude titles itself after the directory it was started in, which is the word the first line already leads with. Drawing it would cost double the height to say the same thing, so what is tested is not 'is there a title' but 'does it say anything the row does not'.

Compared against the label, the directory, the whole path and the harness, because a title matching any of them is a title the reader has already read.

panes: local/w1:p1 place=1 tab=w1:t1 label="muster · claude" hidden

cases.name: a name somebody gave a pane replaces the directory and the harness
cases.why:
A person running fifteen agents wants to say which is which in their own words. Their name wins over anything derived because it is the only line here that was written for this pane rather than worked out from where it happens to be - and it is the durable one: herdr writes a name down, so it survives a daemon restart, where the directory and the harness are re-derived each time (observations/herdr-0.8.0.md section 16).

The raw text travels beside the label so that asking to rename can start from what was typed rather than from a composed label nobody chose.

panes: local/w1:p1 place=1 tab=w1:t1 label="🔥 payments spike" subtitle="first working build" given-name="🔥 payments spike" hidden

cases.name: naming a pane does not cost you the ability to see what it is doing
cases.why:
The two lines answer different questions and both stay: a name is durable identity and a title is volatile status. herdr keeps them as separate fields and setting one never touches the other, so a row that dropped the title on being named would be throwing away something the daemon still holds.

The comparison that suppresses a repeated title now runs against the name, not the directory, because the first line is what the reader actually read.

panes: local/w1:p1 place=1 tab=w1:t1 label="payments spike" given-name="payments spike" hidden

cases.name: a tab carries the name it was given, and an unnamed one carries none
cases.why:
Renaming a tab has to start from what somebody typed, and that is not recoverable from the caption: the caption may carry the tab's workspace in front of the name, and it drops a name that is only digits.

That last rule is why an unnamed tab reports no name at all rather than reporting herdr's own label. herdr labels an unnamed tab with its position inside its workspace, so presence cannot answer 'is this named' - and the same test means a tab somebody names `42` reads as unnamed, which is a limit of herdr's TabInfo rather than a choice made here.

cases.name: the tenth tab is the tenth, not the second
cases.why: The chords name places in this list, so the order it is built in is the order ⌘1 to ⌘9 reach. Ids are opaque strings the backend spells - `w1:t1`, `w1:t10` - and sorting them is numeric order right up until there are ten of something, at which point `w1:t10` lands between `w1:t1` and `w1:t2`. A window with eleven tabs drew them 1, 10, 11, 2, 3 and every numbered chord past the first named the wrong pane. Fifteen panes is this project's own reference workload, so the failure sat exactly where the design says to look. The order is the one the backend listed rather than one derived from the id, which is why this case states its tabs in order and expects them back in it.

cases.name: with the settled scheme a numbered chord names a pane and nothing is left over
cases.why: The half of `numbered_chords` that has to keep working exactly as it did. ⌘2 is the second row down the whole list, one press is the whole gesture, and no press leaves anything behind for the next one to mean something different. This window is arranged so the two schemes disagree - the second pane of the window and the second pane of the second tab are different panes - so a case that passed under either would be pinning nothing.

cases.name: the first press picks a tab and the one after it picks a pane inside that tab
cases.why: The prototype, in one line. Pressing ⌘2 twice reaches the second tab's second pane, which is the fourth pane of the window - so the second press is counting inside the tab the first one named rather than down the list. Both halves are needed to see it: after the first press the chords are counting panes in that tab, and that is what makes the same keystroke mean two things.

pressed: ⌘2 of tabs → tab local/w1:t2 landing on local/w1:p3
⌘2 of panes in local/w1:t2 → pane local/w1:p4

cases.name: reaching a tab lands on its first pane, so ⌘2 alone is ⌘2 ⌘1
cases.why: Where a tab is entered is one rule, shared with clicking its caption and with next_tab, so that three ways of arriving agree. The consequence is worth pinning rather than deriving: the first press is not a half-gesture waiting to be completed, it has already put you somewhere, and the somewhere is the one the second press would have named with a 1.

pressed: ⌘2 of tabs → tab local/w1:t2 landing on local/w1:p3
⌘1 of panes in local/w1:t2 → pane local/w1:p3

cases.name: a third press starts over rather than going a level deeper
cases.why: There is no third level, so the alternative would be a chord that does nothing at all - and a person holding ⌘ and tapping a digit has to be able to predict the third tap. Landing on a pane is what ends the sequence, so ⌘2 ⌘2 ⌘2 is the second tab, its second pane, and the second tab again.

pressed: ⌘2 of tabs → tab local/w1:t2 landing on local/w1:p3
⌘2 of panes in local/w1:t2 → pane local/w1:p4
⌘2 of tabs → tab local/w1:t2 landing on local/w1:p3

cases.name: a second press past the end of its tab does nothing, and the press after it starts over
cases.why: The second tab holds three panes, so ⌘9 after it has nothing to reach. Doing nothing rather than landing on the last pane is the same answer the flat scheme gives, for the same reason - a chord that landed elsewhere as the tab grew would mean something different every time a pane opened. What is new is what it leaves behind: nothing, so the next press is a first press again rather than being stuck counting inside a tab.

pressed: ⌘2 of tabs → tab local/w1:t2 landing on local/w1:p3
⌘1 of tabs → tab local/w1:t1 landing on local/w1:p1

cases.name: a first press past the last tab does nothing, and the window is still counting tabs
cases.why: Two tabs, so ⌘5 reaches nothing. Worth its own case beside the one above because the refusal a person meets is about tabs rather than panes, and because it pins that a press which reached nothing has not quietly armed anything - the press after it is counting tabs, which is where it started.

pressed: ⌘2 of tabs → tab local/w1:t2 landing on local/w1:p3
